1.pericope_label: And he said unto them, Verily I say unto you, That there be some of them that stand here, which shall not taste of death, till they have seen the kingdom of God come with power. And after six days Jesus taketh with him Peter, and James, and John, and leadeth them up into an high mountain apart by themselves: and he was transfigured before them. And his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them. And there appeared unto them Elias with Moses: and they were talking with Jesus. And Peter answered and said to Jesus, Master, it is good for us to be here: and let us make three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias. For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid. And there was a cloud that overshadowed them: and a voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son: hear him. And suddenly, when they had looked round about, they saw no man any more, save Jesus only with themselves. And as they came down from the mountain, he charged them that they should tell no man what things they had seen, till the Son of man were risen from the dead. And they kept that saying with themselves, questioning one with another what the rising from the dead should mean. And they asked him, saying, Why say the scribes that Elias must first come? And he answered and told them, Elias verily cometh first, and restoreth all things; and how it is written of the Son of man, that he must suffer many things, and be set at nought. But I say unto you, That Elias is indeed come, and they have done unto him whatsoever they listed, as it is written of him.

schools.summary: Hold that the chapter division is wrong and the first verse belongs with the discourse before it; lay the problem of its fulfilment out without forcing a settlement, since Luke has them see the kingdom of God, Matthew the Son of man coming as a process, and Mark the kingdom already come and with power, while the second advent plainly did not occur in that generation — so canvass the transfiguration immediately following, the descent of the Spirit at Pentecost, and the destruction of the temple, and leave open whether the same event is meant here as in the verse before. Press the tense, that they should see it not coming but as having actually come in its completeness. Correct the English of the third verse, since the man in question was a scourer whose office was to whiten cloth rather than a fuller who thickened it, note that the words as snow are wanting in the best manuscripts, and call the comparison with clothes fresh from the bleacher's hands peculiar to this evangelist in its homely vividness. Set against all this the rabbinic reading, which takes the promise of the kingdom coming with power as the standing prophetic idiom for vengeance upon the unbelieving nation and lists the scriptural forms it wears — the great and terrible day of the Lord, the end of the world, the last times of that city and dispensation, the beginning of the new world, the coming in the clouds, the enthroning of the twelve to judge the tribes of Israel — and which asks the reader's pardon for doubting that the transfiguration happened on Tabor, since the previous narrative leaves the company in the coasts of Caesarea Philippi with no change of place recorded, no journey is mentioned but only the leading up of three disciples, and it would be strange to undertake so long a march to a mountain never used before when there were mountains near at hand where he commonly resorted.

Date the coming of the kingdom simply to Pentecost, when three thousand were converted at once; report the conjecture that the mountain was one near Caesarea Philippi rather than Tabor or Hermon, and the manuscripts that add the detail of praying; take the Greek word for the change as referring to the form of God and the form of a servant, the indwelling glory let out for a moment; read the overshadowing cloud as the cloud of glory that accompanied Israel in the wilderness and departed, as the Jewish writers say, at the death of Moses, now returning in honour of the greater prophet whom Moses prefigured; and note that the tenth verse is absent from two manuscripts.

Keep to the plain reason for the command of silence, that the mystery shown on the mountain was not to be published before the glory of the passion and the resurrection; and raise a question about Peter's words that the others pass over, whether he spoke in the confusion of his mind by the motion of a spirit not his own, and whether the same spirit that had lately tried to be a stumbling block, so that the passion might be shrunk from, was here working as a seducer under the colour of good.

Reconcile the reckoning of days, since the other evangelist counts in both the day of the saying and the day of the ascent; give the reason for the interval, that the disciples might be filled with a more eager desire during those days and attend with a watchful and anxious mind to what they saw; explain the choice of a mountain rather than a house, the loftiness of the place being suited to the loftiness of the glory shown; and put the disciples' question into plain words — we have seen Elias with thee, and saw thee before we saw Elias, but the scribes say Elias comes first, so we believe they have lied — answering it by the distinction of two advents, of which Elias is forerunner of the second as John was of the first.

Insist that in being transfigured he did not lose the substance of real flesh but showed forth the glory of his own and of our future resurrection, since as he then appeared to the three he will after the judgment appear to all his elect; and offer a second reading of the question about Elias — that the disciples took the change they had seen on the mountain for the coming in glory itself and asked why the forerunner had not appeared, particularly as they had just watched Elias depart. Add that the restoring of all things is what Malachi foretold, and that Elias when he comes must also pay to death the debt his prolonged life has deferred.

Combine the two fulfilments in one account: the kingdom came in power when vengeance was taken for the crucifixion and when the idolatry of the Gentile world was conquered, this being the restoring of a kingdom in a manner lost by the degeneracy of Jews and Gentiles alike; and see the transfiguration as the specimen of it, given six days after the prediction and given for a purpose, since he had begun to tell them of his sufferings and now shows them a glimpse of his glory, to prove that those sufferings were voluntary and to prevent the offence of the cross.

debates.question: What is the kingdom of God coming with power?

sides.position: An open question: the transfiguration that follows, the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, or the destruction of the temple — the second advent plainly did not occur in that generation
The standing prophetic idiom for vengeance on the unbelieving nation, in six scriptural forms
The destruction of the Jewish polity together with the conquest of Gentile idolatry
Pentecost, when three thousand were converted at once
Something already come in its completeness, since the Greek says not coming but come
Not Tabor: the previous narrative leaves the company near Caesarea Philippi, no journey is recorded, and it would be strange to march so far to a mountain never used before
A mountain near Caesarea Philippi, following that argument, rather than Tabor or Hermon
Hermon, whose snow-capped summit may have been visible that very night

debates.question: What were the disciples asking about Elias on the way down?

sides.position: We have seen Elias with thee and saw thee before we saw Elias, but the scribes say Elias comes first, so we conclude they have lied — answered by the distinction of two advents
They took the change on the mountain for the coming in glory and asked why the forerunner had not appeared, having just watched Elias depart
The phrase about rising from the dead had escaped them before and now caught their attention, so they argued over the exegesis of the scribes
Nothing so elaborate: the silence was simply not to publish the mystery before the glory of the passion and resurrection

outliers.note: Alone asks the reader’s pardon for doubting that the transfiguration happened on Tabor, and argues the case from the geography of Galilee and the absence of any recorded journey from Caesarea Philippi.
Alone corrects the English of the third verse, since the man named was a scourer whose office was to whiten cloth rather than a fuller who thickened it.

themes: the kingdom of God come with power

14.pericope_label: And when he came to his disciples, he saw a great multitude about them, and the scribes questioning with them. And straightway all the people, when they beheld him, were greatly amazed, and running to him saluted him. And he asked the scribes, What question ye with them? And one of the multitude answered and said, Master, I have brought unto thee my son, which hath a dumb spirit; And wheresoever he taketh him, he teareth him: and he foameth, and gnasheth with his teeth, and pineth away: and I spake to thy disciples that they should cast him out; and they could not. He answereth him, and saith, O faithless generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you? bring him unto me. And they brought him unto him: and when he saw him, straightway the spirit tare him; and he fell on the ground, and wallowed foaming. And he asked his father, How long is it ago since this came unto him? And he said, Of a child. And ofttimes it hath cast him into the fire, and into the waters, to destroy him: but if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us. Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth. And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. When Jesus saw that the people came running together, he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him. And the spirit cried, and rent him sore, and came out of him: and he was as one dead; insomuch that many said, He is dead. But Jesus took him by the hand, and lifted him up; and he arose. And when he was come into the house, his disciples asked him privately, Why could not we cast him out? And he said unto them, This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting.

schools.summary: Note that this incident is far fuller here than in either parallel, and that it was like the professional scribes to take a keen interest in the failure of the nine, nagging and quizzing them until the party from the mountain arrived to find them at it; list what only this Gospel supplies — the amazement of the crowd, the dumb spirit, the gnashing of the teeth, the pining away, the falling and wallowing, the question how long it had lasted, the fire and the water; work through the verbs one at a time, the word for seizing which gives us catalepsy and which the old physicians used of fits, the word for dashing down, the poetic word for foaming, the word for a shrill squeak, the word for drying up like grass; and observe that the Greek turns the father's own words back on him by making them the subject of the sentence, so that the challenge runs, as to your if thou canst, all things are possible to the believer. Report that the tears and the fasting are both absent from the oldest witnesses.

Locate the fault in the father, who is weak in faith as the reply about believing shows, and who prays in the middle of a crowd while accusing the disciples, and is therefore answered before the same crowd by a charge extended beyond himself to the whole nation, since many of those present had probably been offended and held wrong thoughts about the disciples. Take the command as a proof of divine power, and the words enter no more into him as showing that the spirit was ready to return because the man was weak in faith, and was prevented only by that command.

Read the scene from the side of the two parties present, observing that the scribes are nowhere credited with devotion, faith, humility or reverence, while the whole multitude was amazed and ran and saluted; and reconstruct the question under dispute as being simply why the disciples had been unable to heal the boy set in the midst, which may be gathered from the words that follow. Note that though the sin is reproved the person is not driven off, since the boy is called for at once and brought.

Begin with the puzzle of the tone, since a father pleads for an only son, the need is urgent and the appeal modest, and yet the answer breaks out in a severity quite unlike the usual gentleness — and since the other evangelists give no reason for it, some interpreters have wrongly aimed the rebuke at the disciples or at the father. Decline to make the case merely natural or merely demonic: the term used elsewhere belongs to those seized at the waning of the moon, and the suggestion that the word was a trick of Satan to disgrace the creatures of God must be refused, since experience shows the course of the moon does affect such diseases; Satan had taken the tongue and ears while availing himself of a weakness of brain and nerves already there. Then draw the doctrine from the exchange of conditions, that it is not the Lord who prevents his benefits from flowing in abundance but the narrowness of our faith that lets them come only in drops.

Draw the opposite inference from the address to the spirit, that a natural disease could not properly be commanded to come out of a man and enter no more into him, so that the doctrine of demoniacal influence must be true or the accommodation to vulgar error would be inexplicable; put the emphasis on the pronoun in the charge, since the spirit had resisted the disciples and is now commanded by the master himself; and turn the exchange about faith on the reader, asking why our own souls are not wholly healed and why every demon is not cast out, and answering that he is able and willing but we are not willing to give up our idols.

debates.question: Why is the rebuke so severe when the request was modest?

sides.position: It cannot be aimed at the disciples or the father, as some have supposed; the other evangelists give no reason, and the harshness is against the perverse malice of the nation
It is aimed at the father, weak in faith, who prays in a crowd while accusing the disciples, and is therefore answered before the crowd with a charge extended to all
The dispute was got up by the scribes in the master's absence, and it is they and the failure of the nine that provoke it

debates.question: Was the boy's affliction natural or demonic?

sides.position: Both: the term used elsewhere belongs to those seized at the waning of the moon, and Satan availed himself of a weakness of brain and nerves already there
Demonic, since a natural disease could not properly be commanded to come out and enter no more
A chronic and desperate case of epilepsy with demon possession added; the demon is addressed as a being distinct from the boy

debates.question: Are the words about tears and about fasting genuine?

sides.position: Both are absent from the oldest witnesses; the fasting is a late addition to explain the failure, needless and untrue, since the nine were powerless because they were prayerless
The better manuscripts omit them; the fasting was probably added from an ascetic tendency, as in a like addition elsewhere, though what it teaches is in harmony with the rest of the teaching

outliers.note: Alone refuses to make the case either simply natural or simply demonic, rejecting the suggestion that the name for the disease was a trick of Satan to disgrace the creatures of God, since experience shows the moon does affect such maladies.
Alone denies that the added words about fasting are even true, holding that the nine were powerless because they were prayerless and that their self-complacency spelled defeat.

30.pericope_label: And they departed thence, and passed through Galilee; and he would not that any man should know it. For he taught his disciples, and said unto them, The Son of man is delivered into the hands of men, and they shall kill him; and after that he is killed, he shall rise the third day. But they understood not that saying, and were afraid to ask him. And he came to Capernaum: and being in the house he asked them, What was it that ye disputed among yourselves by the way? But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed among themselves, who should be the greatest. And he sat down, and called the twelve, and saith unto them, If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all. And he took a child, and set him in the midst of them: and when he had taken him in his arms, he said unto them, Whosoever shall receive one of such children in my name, receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me, receiveth not me, but him that sent me.

schools.summary: Explain the privacy of the journey as strategy rather than accident, since he was back in Galilee but avoiding public work there and was no longer the hero of the province; mark the imperfect tense in the disciples' failure to understand, that they continued not to understand and remained agnostic about the death and resurrection even after the mountain; suggest they were afraid to ask because of the bitter memory of the name flung at the chief of them when he protested the last time; read the dispute as being not about the coming death at all but about relative rank in the political kingdom they still expected, so that their silence when questioned was the shame of being found out; and observe that the object lesson did not take, since the twelve wrangle over primacy again and still fail to understand his attitude to children.

Say that they went by the cities rather than through them, along the most private ways, because he wanted time alone with the twelve to instruct them fully concerning his sufferings, and that the delivering up is spoken of as sure as if it were already done; explain their failure to understand as an inability to reconcile the death, and consequently the resurrection which presupposes it, with their notions of a temporal kingdom; gloss the thing disputed bluntly as which of them should be prime minister in that kingdom; and identify the house as the one where he ordinarily lodged.

Harmonise the accounts, since one evangelist has the disciples come and ask who is greatest while here the question is put to them: either that writer began further on and omitted the master's knowledge of their thoughts, or else what they thought and said away from him was as good as said to him, being equally known; and note that a third account has the thought merely entering into them, so that their private discourse was laid open. Allow that the desire itself was not simply forbidden, since the greater a man is the more worthy of honour he becomes.

Observe that sorrowful and joyful things are always mingled, so that sorrow may not frighten by its suddenness but be borne with prepared minds; argue that the ignorance of the disciples proceeded not so much from slowness of intellect as from love, since being still carnal and unacquainted with the mystery of the cross they could not believe that one they had recognised as true God was about to die, and being used to figurative speech took the plain words for another figure; and supply a cause for the quarrel about precedence that the narrative omits, that three had been led apart into the mountain and entrusted with something secret, and the keys had been promised to one of them.

Make the privacy a judgment as well as a preparation: having done many mighty and good works among them in vain, he would not invite them to see more, and turned instead to the disciples, whose approaching trial required them to be made ready; and dwell on the strangeness of the prediction itself, that had he been delivered into the hands of devils and worried by them it had not been so strange, but that men, who have reason and should have love, should be thus spiteful to one who came to redeem them is unaccountable.

Guard the application of the promise from being taken literally, since it cannot be about picking up infants but about showing the least kindness to the meanest believer who resembles a child in humility, meekness and lowliness of mind — and cite the versions that render the phrase one like to this child. Note also that the departure was from the coasts where the mountain stood and the miracle had been wrought, and that the plural reading of the verb is right in sense even where the singular stands, since he did not go alone.

debates.question: Why did he pass through Galilee privately?

sides.position: As a judgment: having done many mighty works there in vain, he would not invite them to see more
Because he was avoiding public work in Galilee now, no longer the hero of the province
Because he wanted time alone with the twelve to instruct them fully concerning his sufferings

debates.question: Why did the disciples not understand the prediction?

sides.position: Not from slowness of intellect but from love, since being still carnal they could not believe that one they had recognised as God was about to die, and took the plain words for a figure
Because they could not reconcile the death, and so the resurrection, with their notions of a temporal kingdom
They continued not to understand, and were afraid to ask, perhaps remembering the name flung at Peter when he protested the last time
Perhaps only the nine are meant, since the three who had seen the transfiguration can hardly have been ignorant after it — and the whole verse is missing from two manuscripts

debates.question: What started the dispute about who was greatest?

sides.position: Three had been led apart into the mountain and entrusted with something secret, and the keys had been promised to one of them
A desire for rank in the political kingdom they still expected, raised first with the master and then pressed further to reach the argument on the road
Plainly which of them should be prime minister in that kingdom

outliers.note: Alone supplies a cause for the quarrel about precedence that the narrative omits, that three had been led apart into the mountain and entrusted with something secret while the keys had been promised to one of them.

Alone notes that the Greek for taking the child in his arms is a single participle found only here and in one later chapter, and that it more probably means the arms were folded round him than that he was lifted up.

themes: the Son of man is delivered

38.pericope_label: And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part. For whosoever shall give you a cup of water to drink in my name, because ye belong to Christ, verily I say unto you, he shall not lose his reward.

schools.summary: Suggest the unlicensed exorcist may have been one of the Baptist's disciples or one of the seventy, and deny there is evidence he was a mere exorcist using the name as a pretence; read the objection unflatteringly, as told to change an embarrassing subject and in expectation of praise, since the saying just before may have raised a doubt about the speaker's own narrowness; or read it as the same zeal that later wanted fire called down on a Samaritan village, offered in self-vindication by a man who had received his master and would receive no one else. Note that the fact reported is historically significant, since it shows the work had quickened spiritual powers outside the circle of disciples: they believed, or they would not have used the Name, and their faith was effective, since they did cast the demons out.

Take the objector to have loved with eminent devotion and to have concluded that a man performing an office he had no right to should be shut out from its benefit, against which the reply establishes that nobody is to be driven away from the partial goodness he already has but rather stirred up toward what he has not yet obtained; and meet the apparent contradiction with the other saying head on, rejecting the escape that one concerns the disciples and the other Christ himself, since a man joined to the disciples as members cannot fail to be with the head — the true answer being that a man is not with him precisely so far as he is against him.

Reason that a man who knew nothing of Christ could scarcely work a miracle in his name, and settle on the same two possibilities, adding that one of the seventy might have left the company after his commission while keeping his faith and so keeping the power; prefer the reading not against you and point to the parallel where Joshua asked Moses to forbid two men prophesying in the camp; take the whole as a rebuke of bigotry, since some are so wedded to their own creed that they would rather let sinners perish than see men who differ become the instruments of their salvation; and reconcile the two proverbs by their purposes, the one warning that no neutrality is possible in the war with Satan, the other directing us to judge candidly, so that we should be rigorous in judging ourselves and candid in judging each other.

Clear the objector of jealousy or envy, holding that he wished everyone who called on the name to follow and be one body with the rest; observe that many believers received gifts without being with Christ, some pure in life but imperfect in faith and others the reverse; and explain the reply, that however unworthy those who perform the miracles may be, others are incited by their means to believe, and the workers themselves are induced by that unspeakable grace to become better. Note the force of the word quickly in the promise, which allows for those who afterwards fell into heresy.

Be more suspicious than the rest, allowing that the man may have acted with no bad intention but judging that he had rashly taken, or rather seized upon, an office never given him, since this power was bestowed only on those chosen to be heralds of the Gospel — while granting that his boldness was not without success, God being pleased in this way also to throw lustre round his name, as he sometimes does by ministries he does not approve as lawful. Then guard the concession carefully: this is no licence for rash men to intermeddle and disturb the whole order of the church, and those who hold a middle place between enemies and friends are not thereby acknowledged as disciples, but are only reckoned useful so far as they do no harm.

debates.question: Who was the man casting out devils in the name?

sides.position: One of the Baptist's disciples or one of the seventy; there is no evidence he was a mere exorcist using the name as a pretence
One of the seventy who had left the company after his commission while keeping his faith, and so keeping the power
A former disciple of John, baptized into the name of a Messiah shortly to come, who cast out devils in the name of Messiah and did not follow from ignorance rather than contempt
Possibly a man who had rashly seized an office never given him, though God was pleased to throw lustre round his name even so

debates.question: What was the motive of the objection?

sides.position: Not jealousy or envy, but a wish that all who called on the name should follow and be one body with the rest
Eminent devotion, concluding that a man performing an office he had no right to should be shut out from its benefit
The same zeal that later wanted fire called down on a Samaritan village, offered as self-vindication
An attempt to change an embarrassing subject, told in expectation of praise

debates.question: How does he that is not against us agree with he that is not with me?

sides.position: A man is not with him precisely so far as he is against him; the escape that one saying concerns the disciples and the other Christ will not do, since one joined to the members cannot fail to be with the head
The two proverbs have different purposes: one warns that no neutrality is possible in the war with Satan, the other directs us to judge men candidly
Both are needed; some imagine themselves for Christ who refuse to take a stand in the open with him
The saying is no licence for rash men to disturb the order of the church, and does not acknowledge such men as disciples, only as useful so far as they do no harm

outliers.note: Alone reconstructs the exorcist as a former disciple of John who cast out devils in the name of Messiah rather than of Jesus, and whose not following was ignorance rather than contempt.
Alone treats the apparent contradiction between the two proverbs as a problem to be solved rather than a difference of occasion, and works through and rejects the easy escape before answering it.

themes: a cup of water to drink

42.pericope_label: And whosoever shall offend one of these little ones that believe in me, it is better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he were cast into the sea. And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. And if thy foot offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter halt into life, than having two feet to be cast into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out: it is better for thee to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

schools.summary: Distinguish the word here from the other term also rendered hell, and explain the valley whose name it bears; report that the oldest and best manuscripts lack two of the three occurrences of the refrain about the worm and the fire, which came in from later families as a mere repetition of the third, and that this is why two verse numbers are missing from the modern text; trace the words almost verbatim to the last verse of Isaiah, where the worshippers go out to look on the carcases of the transgressors, and take the imagery from a battlefield, the worm feeding while there are bodies to devour and the fire burning until they are consumed. On the valley itself, either state as fact that it was desecrated by the sacrifice of children and used for the city garbage where worms gnawed and fires burned, or allow it only as a possibility and warn that the authorities are hardly definite enough to warrant the positive statement. Suppose no real worm and perhaps no material fire, the whole being a figure for destruction awful, wide-spread and eternal.

Take the hand for the close friend whose help we daily require, and conclude that such a man must be driven from our society if he would hurt us in what concerns the soul, lest by choosing a portion in this life with one who is lost we perish together with him in the next; and weigh the great question carefully rather than settling it, reporting those who assign both worm and fire to the soul and read the fire as burning grief, on the strength of the apostle asking who is offended and he burns not, then judging it more credible that there will be pain of body and of soul alike, and concluding that it is easier to say both belong to the body than that neither does. Take the middle course as well, the worm accusing inwardly and the fire raging without.

Mark the transition, that the discourse has moved from the case of giving offence to that of taking it, so that one who is as useful or dear to us as a hand or eye but hinders us in the ways of God is to be renounced — the saying relating primarily to persons and only secondarily to things; report the clause about unquenchable fire as absent from several witnesses at more than one place; and name the particular gnawings meant by the worm, pride, self-will, desire, malice, envy, shame, sorrow and despair, which no more die than the soul itself does.

State flatly that this is said not of our limbs but of our intimate friends, whom we look on as limbs because we need them, since nothing is so hurtful as mischievous society; deny that a visible worm is meant and identify it with conscience gnawing the soul for the good it has not done, so that each man is made his own accuser by calling to mind what he did in this mortal life and his worm remains for ever; and compare the apostle's word that the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is.

Keep the wider sense of parting with whatever is nearest, and supply the rabbinic background, that the Jewish canons prescribed cutting off the hand in certain cases, language never meant for execution but framed to show the heinousness of the crime, to express abhorrence of it, and to deter men from it — better, as the gloss says, that the hand be cut off than that a man be guilty of such evil. Then identify the worm with conscience and press it into detail: it will fly in the sinner's face, accuse, upbraid, aggravate and never cease, so that the soul in torment shall never die nor lose any of its powers.

debates.question: Do the hand, foot and eye mean limbs or people?

sides.position: Not our limbs but our intimate friends, whom we look on as limbs because we need them
The close friend whose help we daily require, who must be driven from our society if he would hurt us in what concerns the soul
Primarily persons and only secondarily things, the discourse having moved from giving offence to taking it
Whatever is nearest and dearest, the rabbinic canons prescribing amputation being framed to show the heinousness of a crime rather than for execution

debates.question: Are the worm and the fire literal?

sides.position: No visible worm: it is conscience gnawing the soul for the good it has not done, so that each man is his own accuser
Conscience, flying in the sinner's face, accusing, upbraiding, aggravating, never ceasing
The particular gnawings are pride, self-will, desire, malice, envy, shame, sorrow and despair
No real worm and perhaps no material fire; a figure for destruction awful, wide-spread and eternal
More credible that there will be pain of body and of soul alike, and easier to say both belong to the body than that neither does
The worm accuses inwardly while the fire rages without

debates.question: Was the Valley of Hinnom actually the city's burning refuse heap?

sides.position: Yes: desecrated by the sacrifice of children, it was used for the city garbage where worms gnawed and fires burned
Possibly, but the authorities are hardly definite enough to warrant the positive statement

outliers.note: Alone checks the familiar claim about the Valley of Hinnom, allowing it as a possibility while warning that the authorities are hardly definite enough to warrant the positive statement.

Alone weighs at length whether the worm and the fire belong to the soul or the body, reporting the arguments for reading the fire as burning grief before concluding it is easier to say both belong to the body than that neither does.

49.pericope_label: For every one shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt. Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another.

schools.summary: Concede that perhaps no passage in the New Testament has given commentators more perplexity and that it may now be impossible to fix its meaning; report that many of the best copies omit the second clause while one of the best omits the first, as though transcribers felt either clause more intelligible alone than the two together; set out three objections to the reading that makes the salting a preservation in torment — that it arbitrarily narrows the every one of the sentence to the finally condemned, that it is scarcely conceivable the one word should carry contrasted senses within a single verse, and that it runs against the uniform symbolism of salt elsewhere as what purifies and preserves from taint; suspect the verse may have no reference to future punishment at all, the difficulty having arisen from reading it as a reason for what precedes rather than as part of the chapter's argument about tolerance; and note that salt gone flat cannot be seasoned by anything and is fit to season nothing, an exploded shell, a burnt-out crater, a spent force.

Reject the emendation that would make the text read every sacrifice of flour, and restrict the subject instead: every one means not every man but every one of those whose worm dieth not, so that they are seasoned with fire and become unconsumable, enduring for ever to be tormented as salt preserves flesh from corruption — a sense supported from the Jewish comment on the same verse of Isaiah. Or take the sacrificial sense, that believers are exhorted to offer themselves now to be seasoned and made devoted offerings, on the model of the law requiring every meat offering to be salted, and that they are salted by the word of the Gospel; then add the caution that since salt bites by its sharpness the seasoning must be regulated so that peace is preserved entire.

Refuse to choose between the two readings and take both, so that the man who will not part with hand or eye is salted with a fire which preserves rather than consumes him, while the willing sacrifice is salted with grace, which purifies the soul, though frequently with pain, and preserves it from corruption; call the emendation of the first clause taking the text by storm; quote the old commentator who has the Spirit as salt drying up the bad humours in us that breed the never-dying worm; and read the final charge as the proof that will satisfy their own minds and silence the world, since living in brotherly kindness shows them free from the ambition that began the whole discourse.

sides.position: Not every man but every one of those whose worm dieth not, seasoned so as to become unconsumable and endure for ever to be tormented

Both classes at once: the man who will not part with hand or eye salted with a preserving fire, the willing sacrifice salted with grace
Believers, exhorted to offer themselves now to be seasoned as devoted sacrifices, on the model of the law of the meat offering
Possibly nobody in that sense, since the verse may have no reference to future punishment at all and the difficulty comes of tying it to the verse before
